title: Stacks and Monotonic Stacks
summary: Last in, first out: the right tool for nesting, undo, expression parsing, and next-greater questions.
keyPoints: A stack supports push and pop at one end, both O(1).
Use a stack whenever the most recent unfinished item must be handled first.
A monotonic stack keeps values increasing or decreasing to answer next-greater or next-smaller questions in O(n).
Expression parsing uses a stack for operators or intermediate results.

complexity.note: Each index is pushed and popped once.
Worst case is all opening brackets.

commonMistakes: Popping an empty stack without checking first.
Matching every closing bracket with the most recent opening bracket of any type instead of the matching type.
Using a monotonic stack but storing values instead of indices when distance is needed.
Forgetting that a stack can also model recursion and tree traversal.
interviewNotes: Say why the most recent item is the correct one to handle next.
For monotonic stacks, explain what the stack contains after each step and why popped items need no further work.
For parsing, clarify operator precedence and whether division/multiplication is left-associative.

checkYourself.question: Why is a stack the natural fit for nested brackets?
checkYourself.answer: The most recently opened bracket must close before any earlier one. That is exactly last-in, first-out order.

checkYourself.question: In a monotonic decreasing stack for next greater element, what do the indices represent?
checkYourself.answer: They are values still waiting for a larger element. When a larger value arrives, it is the answer for every smaller value on the stack.

checkYourself.question: How does a stack help evaluate postfix notation?
checkYourself.answer: Operands are pushed. When an operator appears, pop the required operands, apply the operator, and push the result.
